Because the intense sound of the morning Muracam drum
Sounded at the palace of the Pāṇṭiyaṉ [with] a garland and a parasol
Who ruled [his] wide kingdom; so that [even] the kings [of] the cool groves
Of Nāvalam; [and] the tiger [= Cōḻas] and the bow [= Cēras]
Who marked [their signs] on the forehead of the Himalayas
Beside [= secondary to] the carp [= the Pāṇṭiya symbol];
[All] listen to [the Pāṇṭiyaṉ’s] command,
Aiyai, saying, ‘The turn [to supply] ghee for us is today’,
Having called out to her daughter,
The elderly lady [from] the middle-clan would arrive [at the scene],
Having come, carrying a churning-rope [and] a churning staff.

[Aiyai says]
The milk [in] the pot does not curdle. Innocent tears
Of the bull [with] a heap[-like] hump pour forth.
Something is coming.
The fragrant butter [on the pots suspended by] ropes
Melts without being made to melt. The goats
Do not play [anymore], jumping about.
Something is coming.
The herd of four-breasted [cows], shaking, stand [in one place],
Depressed. [Their] large bells fall off [their necks].
Something is coming.

div.p: kuṭattuppā luṟaiyāmaiyum kuviyimilēṟṟiṉ maṭakkaṇṇīr cōrtalum uṟiyilveṇṇe yurukāmaiyum maṟi muṭaṅki yāṭāmaiyum māṉmaṇi nilattaṟṟu vīḻtalum varuvatōr tuṉpamuṇṭeṉa makaḷainōkki maṉamayaṅkātē maṇṇiṉ mātark kaṇiyākiya kaṇṇakiyun tāṉkāṇa āyar pāṭiyileru maṉṟattu māyavaṉuṭaṉ tammuṉāṭiya vālacaritai nāṭakaṅkaḷil vēṉeṭuṅkaṭ piññaiyōṭāṭiya kuravaiyāṭutum yāmeṉṟāḷ kaṟavaikaṉṟu tuyar nīṅkuka veṉavē

Saying, ‘The milk in the pot not curdling, the pouring forth of innocent tears by the bull [with] a heap[-like] hump, the white butter [suspended in a pot by a] rope not melting, the goats, bending over, not playing, the great bell falling-having been cut off-to the ground, there is a sorrowful thing that comes,’ looking at [her] daughter, she [Aiyai] not getting perturbed [in her] mind, said, ‘As Kaṇṇaki who is an ornament to the lady of the earth watches, we shall dance the Kuravai that Piññai [with] spear[-like] long eyes danced in the dramatic passages in the Bālacarita that the elder brother (Balarāma) danced with Māyavaṉ upon the dung[-covered] village common, so that misery may leave the calves [of] the milk-cows.’

mallaṉ maḻa viṭai yūrntāṟ kuriyaḷ immullaiyam pūm kuḻal tāṉ
nuṇ poṟi veḷḷai yaṭarttāṟkē yākum ippeṇ koṭi mātar taṉ tōḷ
poṉ poṟi veḷḷai yaṭarttāṟkē yākum innal koṭi mel mulai tāṉ
veṉṟi maḻa viṭai yūrntāṟ kuriyaḷ ikkoṉṟaiyam pūm kuḻalāḷ
tū niṟa veḷḷai yaṭarttāṟ kuriyaḷ ip pūvaip putu malarāḷ
This girl with a garland of lake flowers who has desire for him who mounted-[being] one who was not afraid-the black bull —
[Such are your] designations;
The shoulders of this golden-braceleted beauty to whom he who conquered [the bull with] the red mark [on] the forehead has a right;
She—this [girl with] curls [with] Mullai flowers—to whom he who mounted [as] a warrior] the young [= untamed] bull has a right;
The shoulders of this beauty [like] a girl [as] a creeper are suitable only for him who conquered the white bull [with] fine spots;
The soft breasts of her—this good creeper—are suitable only for him who conquered the white bull [with] gold spots;
This girl with curls [that have] laburnum flowers is suitable for him who mounted the victorious, young bull;
This girl with fresh bilberry flowers is suitable for him who conquered the white bull [with] a pure colour;

Thus, saying that
The seven girls—the girls with young garlands
Raised, having intended upon (one), the bulls [in] the cattleshed(?),
Looking at her daughter, positioning [the seven girls] in the ancient order,
The elderly lady of the middle-clan would give them [each] an invented name.
The names the the girls desired were Kural, Tuttam, Kaikkiḷai, Uḻai,
Iḷi, Viḷari [and] Tāram, starting [in] the west, [going in] a lefward order.
She said ‘Māyavaṉ’ to [the girl called] Kural. She said ‘Victorious, white Āyavaṉ’
To the Iḷi one. To the singular Tuttam, she said ‘[You] will be the cowherdress Piṉṉai.’
She said the order [of] the others is [in] front.
Those of the measure [= of the same status] of Māyavaṉ are Piṉṉai and Tāram.
Those of the measure of the pure white one [= Āyavaṉ] are Uḻai and Viḷari.
Kaikkiḷai is [to] the left of Piṉṉai.
The good Viḷari is to the right of the aforementioned [= Iḷi].
Among them, [the elderly lady] putting a Tulasi garland on Māyavaṉ,
Would make happen the unhindering Kuravai. Saying,
‘The one who measured the world [with] the excellence [he] possessed
Not looking at Tiru on his own chest, it seems our Piṉṉai —
—with hands from which bangles cascade—is his!
The cowherdress’ daughter said ‘Wow!’

p.head: The taking place of the dance.

[Among] those — the girls who were selected [for] the excellence of the dancing in that state,
[They] having strung together [their] hands [in] the crab gesture, with [the formation of]
A perfect circle, the creeper[-girl] Kural—in the front—looking at her [who was Kural’s] musical fifth [Iḷi],
Said, ‘let us sing the sweet number [in] the Mullai melody [about] him who broke
The Kuruntu tree in the wide fields [of] the clearings!
Saying so,
Kural being of a low [pitch/volume], Iḷi being of a moderate [pitch/volume]
[And] Tuttam being strong, the girl who holds the Viḷari which was not strong
[And thus] moderate, would [now] take up the [pitch of] the song
After [following the cue/pitch] of her musical fourth (Tuttam).

Oh friend, won't we hear the sweet Koṉrai flute on [his] mouth
When he comes among our cattle today - Māyavaṉ who scattered
The fruits [from the tree], [using] a calf [as] a beating stick!
Oh friend, won't we hear the sweet Āmpal flute on [his] mouth
When he comes over here among our cattle - Māyavaṉ who churned
The ocean, [using] a snake as a churning rope!
Oh friend, won't we hear the sweet Mullai flute on [his] mouth
When he comes among our cattle at dusk -- Māyavaṉ who broke
The Kuruntu tree on the mountain slopes [of the region with] clearings!
We will [now] sing of the beautiful colour of Piṉṉai
Who played with him of the ghat of Yamunā!
Do we sing about him who hid the clothes [of the girls with]
The grace [= waists], about to break and tender, having swayed?
Or do we sing about the faces [of the ladies] of fragrant, tender grace
Who are frantic, [because of] him who hid [their] clothes?
Do we sing about the full figure of her whose heart was stolen
Among the floods of the Yamunā river, [by] him who committed deceit?
Or, do we sing about the [beautiful] form of him who committed deceit
[Towards] the fullness and the bangles of her whose heart was stolen?
Do we sing about the face of the girl who hid [herself] in [her] hands
Having lost [her] clothes and jewels?
Or, do we sing about the [beautiful] form of him who bore
[The pangs of] mad love, having become distressed, seeing the face
Of her who hid [herself] in [her] hands?

Nārataṉār who studies the ancient Vedas
Will look after the musical measure of Piññai
[with] flower-tresses in which buds open,
Who is to the left of him of the colour of the ocean
Who hid the rays [of the sun] with [his] discus -- [and]
Who is to the right of his elder brother [with] a fragrant body
That resembles the moon; [and] he will thrum the strings
[Of an instrument] in the ancient order/manner.
Nārataṉār among the musical orchestra will look after the measure
Of our Piṉṉai who bent [her] neck [adorned with a] jewel-clasp
Who is to the left of Māyavaṉ [with] a body that resembles the neck of a peacock;
[And] He will thrum the strings [of an instrument with]
Musical measures that unite [with] the melody.

As for the Kuravai Māyavaṉ dances at the village arena
Along with his older brother and Piṉṉai [with] arms [with] striped bangles
[The girls with] choice bangles having tapped/moved [their] feet
To the beat of the music, As Yaśoda praises [them]
As the garland [on] the curls [= heads] of the little girls
Of the cowherds droops down [their] backs,
It is befitting!
Hey friend! Let us praise, let us praise
The God who mounts the bird, having a song of the Uḷvari type
Of [only] one rhythmic sequence. (?)

The garland of sandal that is not strung
The pearl string [from] the ocean that is strung
[And] the garland worn by the king of the Gods -- these [garlands]
Are [on] the chest of the Southern king [= Pāṇṭiya]. Indeed, they say
The one who wore the garland that is worn by the king of the Gods
Is the one who broke the Kuruntu trees, having grazed [as one among]
The clan of the cowherds, in prosperous Dvāraka.
The king who lives in fortified Pukār - the king Vaḷavaṉ -
Is the one who ruled the earth, having impressed the tiger
Upon the peak of the golden Himalaya. Indeed, they say
That] king who lives in fortified Pukār - the King Vaḷavaṉ
Is him with the fighting weapon [of] a golden discus.
The king who lives in wealthy Vañci - the king Cēraṉ -
Is the one who overthrew the Kaṭampa tree that could never die,
Having entered into the three [kinds of] wateres [= the ocean].
Indeed, they say that the king who leaves in wealthy Vañci -
The king Cēraṉ - is him who crossed the oceans, having raised
[His] shoulders that resembled mountains.
